Part 5 of Block Diffusion RooflinesPrevious: 4 · The attention partNext: 6 · Calculator

Parts 3 and 4 treat the two extremes, a pass that reads only weights and one that reads only KV cache. This chapter covers every context in between: it states when TD wins (Proposition 7) and the batch it needs to saturate compute (Proposition 8), sorts the cases into eight regimes, compares accelerators and models, and shows the exact gain over batch and context.

Proposition 2 makes each intensity a byte-weighted average of its linear part (Part 3) and its attention part (Part 4). Putting them back into Proposition 1 gives the general answer.

Proposition 7When TD wins

In short. TD wins exactly when a pass serves more tokens per read than it pays in penalty (\(\mathrm{TPF} \ge \Pi\)) and AR uses at most a fraction \(1/\omega\) of the compute (\(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} \le I^\star/\omega\)).

Assume (A1) to (A5), and write \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}\) and \(\Pi\) with the shares of an AR step's bytes, as in Proposition 2: \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} = \class{mj-ar}{\theta^{AR}_{\mathrm{lin}}}\class{mj-ar}{I^{AR}_{\mathrm{lin}}} + \class{mj-ar}{\theta^{AR}_{\mathrm{attn}}}\class{mj-ar}{I^{AR}_{\mathrm{attn}}}\) and \(\Pi - 1 = \class{mj-ar}{\theta^{AR}_{\mathrm{lin}}}(\Pi_{\mathrm{lin}} - 1) + \class{mj-ar}{\theta^{AR}_{\mathrm{attn}}}(\Pi_{\mathrm{attn}} - 1)\). By Corollary 1, TD loses if AR is compute-bound (\(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} \ge I^\star\)), and otherwise \(\Gamma = \min\bigl(\mathrm{TPF}/\Pi,\ I^\star/(\omega \class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}})\bigr)\). In the second case:

  1. \(\Gamma \ge 1\) exactly when both \(\mathrm{TPF} \ge \Pi\) and \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} \le I^\star/\omega\): a TD pass must serve more tokens per read than it pays in penalty, and AR must use at most a fraction \(1/\omega\) of the compute, so that TD's \(\omega\) times more FLOPs fit in what AR leaves idle.
  2. Treat \(B\) as a real variable and assume that \(\Pi(\cdot, C)\) is non-increasing in \(B\). Since \(\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(B)/B\) is non-increasing (proof of Proposition 4), \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}(\cdot, C)\) is non-decreasing in \(B\), and \(\Gamma\) is maximal at the batch \(\class{mj-td}{B^\star_{TD}}(C)\) at which \(\class{mj-td}{I_{TD}} = I^\star\), or at \(B = 1\) if \(\class{mj-td}{I_{TD}}(1, C) \ge I^\star\). Over integer batches the maximum is at \(\lfloor \class{mj-td}{B^\star_{TD}}(C)\rfloor\) or \(\lceil \class{mj-td}{B^\star_{TD}}(C)\rceil\). The assumption on \(\Pi\) can fail: for \(b = 8\), \(\Pi_{\mathrm{lin}}\) is 3.52 at batch 1 and 3.70 at batch 2 (Part 3).
Proof

(1) A minimum of two numbers is at least 1 exactly when both are. (2) The first term of the minimum is non-decreasing in \(B\) and the second is non-increasing. The minimum of two such functions is maximal where they cross, which is where \(\class{mj-td}{I_{TD}} = b\,\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}/\Pi = I^\star\), or at \(B = 1\) if the first is already the larger there. Over integer batches the minimum is non-decreasing up to \(\lfloor \class{mj-td}{B^\star_{TD}}(C)\rfloor\) and non-increasing from \(\lceil \class{mj-td}{B^\star_{TD}}(C)\rceil\) on. \(\blacksquare\)

Proposition 7 specialises as follows. At short context \(\Pi = \Pi_{\mathrm{lin}}\) and \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} = \class{mj-ar}{I^{AR}_{\mathrm{lin}}}(B)\), so the first condition of Proposition 7(1) is a lower bound on the batch (the linear penalty must fall below TPF) and the second an upper bound (\(B_\times\)). At long context \(\Pi = \Pi_{\mathrm{attn}}\) and \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} = \class{mj-ar}{I^{AR}_{\mathrm{attn}}}\), and neither condition depends on the batch. For DiffusionGemma on an H200, both conditions hold at every batch up to 109 at short context, and at every batch at long context.

Proposition 8The batch needed to saturate compute

In short. With dense attention and full windows, a batch cannot saturate compute on cache bytes, since each sequence brings its own cache, but a canvas can: once \(b\,I_{\mathrm{attn}} \gt I^\star\), a longer context makes a TD pass compute-bound at a smaller batch, not a larger one.

Let \(B^\star_n(C)\) be the smallest batch at which a pass with \(n\) queries per sequence (\(n = 1\) for AR, \(n = b\) for TD) is compute-bound, or \(\infty\) if there is none, with dense attention and the windows full (\(C \ge w\)). Write \(I_n\) and \(W_n\) for the intensity and the weights of that pass: \(I_1 = \class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}\), \(W_1 = \class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}\), \(I_b = \class{mj-td}{I_{TD}}\), \(W_b = \class{mj-td}{W_{TD}}\).

  1. If \(n\,I_{\mathrm{attn}} \lt I^\star\), then \(B^\star_n(C)\) is non-decreasing in \(C\), and infinite beyond some finite context.
  2. If \(n\,I_{\mathrm{attn}} \gt I^\star\), then \(B^\star_n(C)\) is non-increasing in \(C\), and equal to 1 beyond some finite context.

AR is in the first case whenever \(I_{\mathrm{attn}} \lt I^\star\), which holds for every model and accelerator of Tables 8 and 9. TD is in the second case exactly when \(b \gt b_c = I^\star/I_{\mathrm{attn}}\), the critical canvas length.

Proof

Write \(D_n(C) = n\,\class{mj-ar}{F^{AR}}(C) - I^\star \class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}_{\mathrm{attn}}}(C)\). Multiplying out \(I_n \ge I^\star\) gives \(B\,D_n(C) \ge I^\star s_wW_n(B)\): each sequence contributes \(n\class{mj-ar}{F^{AR}}\) FLOPs, of which \(I^\star \class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}_{\mathrm{attn}}}\) are needed to make its own cache reads compute-bound, and what is left, summed over the batch, has to cover the weights. The right side is positive, so no batch works when \(D_n \le 0\). For \(C \ge w\), \(D_n\) is affine in \(C\) with slope \((nI_{\mathrm{attn}} - I^\star)\,\nu_G\). A smaller \(D_n\) can only remove batches from the feasible set, so a negative slope makes \(B^\star_n\) non-decreasing and eventually infinite; a positive slope makes the set grow until batch 1 works, once \(D_n \ge I^\star s_wW_n(1)\). Nothing needs a closed form for \(W_n(B)\), so the argument covers MoE models. \(\blacksquare\)

The canvas does for the KV cache what batch does for the weights.

A larger batch does not help with cache bytes, because every sequence brings its own cache. AR uses each cache byte for one query, so at long context its intensity tends to \(I_{\mathrm{attn}}\), far below the ridge, whatever the batch. A canvas uses each cache byte for \(b\) queries, and once \(b\,I_{\mathrm{attn}} \gt I^\star\) a longer context makes compute easier to saturate, not harder. When \(W_n\) does not depend on \(B\), solving the inequality gives \(B^\star_n(C) = \lceil I^\star s_wW_n/D_n(C)\rceil\) for \(D_n \gt 0\), which at zero context is the \(\class{mj-ar}{B^\star_{AR}}\) and \(\class{mj-td}{B^\star_{TD}}\) of Part 3.

Figure 15

As the context grows, the batch at which a pass turns compute-bound falls for a canvas of 256 and rises for AR (Proposition 8).

Here \(I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 8\) and \(b_c = 206/8 \approx 26\). AR needs a batch of 1,640 at zero context, and past 135 tokens no batch is enough (\(B\,D_1(C) \ge I^\star s_w\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(B)\) of Proposition 8 then has no solution). TD with \(b = 256\) needs 6.4 at zero context, and batch 1 is enough from about 224k tokens. TD with \(b = 32\) first needs a slightly larger batch while the windows fill (\(b\,I_{\mathrm{win}} = 64 \lt I^\star\)), then a smaller one once global attention dominates (\(b\,I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 256 \gt I^\star\)). TD with \(b = 16\) is below \(b_c\) and behaves like AR. The grey region is where the weights and the batch's cache exceed the H200's 141 GB: at 1k tokens about 390 sequences fit, far below the 1,640 that AR would need, so for DiffusionGemma on an H200 AR decoding is memory-bound at every batch that fits.

Eight regimes

Each minimum in Proposition 1 asks whether one decoder is compute- or memory-bound. Answering both questions at short context (\(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} = \class{mj-ar}{I^{AR}_{\mathrm{lin}}}\), \(\Pi = \Pi_{\mathrm{lin}}\)) and at long context with dense attention (\(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} = I_{\mathrm{attn}}\), \(\Pi = 1\)) gives eight regimes. Four of them are the ones of Parts 3 and 4; the other four need AR compute-bound, which no batch that fits in memory achieves here.

  • AR compute-bound (R3, R4, R7, R8). TD loses, with \(\Gamma \le 1/\omega\): in R4 and R8 both decoders run at peak and only the work ratio is left, and in R3 and R7 a TD pass is memory-bound and slower still.
  • Both memory-bound (R1, R5). TD's extra FLOPs hide under the memory time, and each read serves TPF tokens, at the penalty of whichever part dominates.
  • AR memory-bound, TD compute-bound (R2, R6). TD uses compute that AR leaves idle, \(\Gamma = I^\star/(\omega \class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}})\), independent of \(b\); it falls with the batch at short context (inversely proportional to \(B\) once AR touches every expert) and is flat in the batch at long context.
Remark 2Kernels run one after another

In short. Timing a pass as a chain of kernels instead of one fully overlapped kernel is never faster and at most twice as slow; on an H200 it moves DiffusionGemma's best batch from 5 to 9.

(A1) gives a pass the time of one kernel in which all of its compute and memory traffic overlap. A pass is a chain of kernels, and adding their roofline times, \(\sum_c \max(F_c/\pi, Q_c/\beta)\) over kernel classes, is never faster and at most twice as slow. For an AR step at moderate batch every class is memory-bound and nothing changes. For a TD pass the dense layers are compute-bound from batch 1 while the experts stay memory-bound until \(Bbk/E \approx I^\star\), batch 13 here; at context 1k on an H200 the best batch moves from 5 to 9 and the peak gain from 5.3× to 3.8× (Figure 10). The calculator offers both rules.

Across accelerators and models

Figure 17 · interactive

The gain depends on the accelerator only through its ridge point.

The curve is the gain for a chip of ridge point \(I^\star = \pi/\beta\); each dot is an accelerator. Drag the marker along the axis, select a dot, or switch to long context.

Exact roofline gains, DiffusionGemma, BF16, \(b = 256\), \(S = 14\). Multiplying the peak \(\pi\) and the bandwidth \(\beta\) by the same factor divides the time of every pass by the same factor, so \(\Gamma\) depends on the accelerator only through \(I^\star\), and the accelerators lie on the curve. Over this range a higher ridge point never lowers the gain, at short or at long context. Short context: \(C = 1{,}024\), at the batch that maximises \(\Gamma\); on the flat stretch near \(I^\star = 60\), batch 1 is best and both decoders are memory-bound, so the gain is \(\mathrm{TPF}/\Pi\) whatever the ridge. Long context: \(C = 2^{20}\) at batch 1; the dashed line is the limit \(I^\star/(\omega I_{\mathrm{attn}})\) as \(C \to \infty\), linear in \(I^\star\). Over this range the curve lies above the line, because at batch 1 the weights are still about a quarter of an AR step's bytes; above \(I^\star \approx 620\) a TD pass at batch 1 is itself memory-bound at this context, and the curve is flat. The curve assumes unlimited memory; a hollow dot marks an accelerator in which the model and its KV cache do not fit. Both axes are logarithmic.

Each model below is paired with a hypothetical TD twin on the same backbone (\(r = 1\), no self-conditioning). Dense models pay no linear penalty, so at batch 1 the gain is \(\min(\mathrm{TPF},\ I^\star/\omega)\): 13.7 on an H200, where a dense TD pass is already compute-bound. Their AR intensity also grows fastest with the batch. MoE models pay a linear penalty close to their ratio of total to active parameters. The long-context limit depends only on \(I_{\mathrm{attn}}\), or on \(I_{\mathrm{idx}}\) for the sparse variant.

The exact maps

The maps drop the propositions' simplifications and use the exact accounting (appendix), vocabulary included, over batch × context. Every line is a contour of the computed grid. Faded cells do not fit in the accelerator's memory, which must hold the weights, the KV cache and one pass's logits, \(b\) times larger for a TD canvas than for an AR step. On the gain maps, faded colour marks where TD does not fit, and hatching where AR does not fit either. Hover or tap a cell for its values.

Figure 20 · interactive

At context 1k AR catches up with TD at batch 110, and at a larger batch as the context grows, beyond 1,024 from 64k tokens on.An AR step never reaches the ridge, and at long context its intensity tends to 8 whatever the batch.A TD canvas crosses the ridge at a batch that falls as the context grows, from 5 at 1k to 1 at 256k, and its intensity tends to 2,048.With sparse global layers, AR catches up with TD near batch 90–110 at every context up to 1M tokens.

As the context grows, \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}\) tends to \(I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 8\) without reaching the ridge, and \(\class{mj-td}{I_{TD}}\) tends to \(b\,I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 2{,}048\), above it. On the gain map, the bottom-left is R1, the band above the TD-compute line is R2, and the colour flattens toward R6's 1.7 at long context. With sparse layers it falls further at large batch, toward the sparse limit 0.86 given after Table 6, and stays between 2.3 and 2.6 at batch 1, where the weights still carry most of AR's bytes.
